Outcome · Product performance
Improving a mature component is the hardest kind of engineering, and the most valuable.

Across the automotive industry, engineering teams are under pressure to deliver high-performing, energy-efficient products at an ever faster pace. They must balance complex trade-offs against manufacturing constraints and tight timelines, while traditional design processes slow them down with long iteration cycles.

Neural Concept’s Engineering AI copilots, tailored to MAHLE’s own data and processes, explored more than 30 million virtual blower designs in record time. MAHLE’s engineers set the performance goals, domain constraints and design parameters. The copilots instantly predicted real-world performance and proposed geometries that met or exceeded the specification.

Aerodynamics, noise and efficiency across millions of variants were all accessible in a single interface. Development moved from sequential, time-consuming iterations to a continuous, AI-assisted co-design process, guided by MAHLE’s engineers at every step.
Dr. Uli Christian Blessing · Vice President Product Development, Thermal and Fluid Systems · MAHLE · Neural Concept Connect 2025

Unveiled at Auto Shanghai 2025, the new blower creates a more compact, symmetrical air-conditioning unit, an edge in EVs where space is at a premium. It also cements MAHLE’s leadership on one of its most widely used components.
MAHLE is set to establish processes to use AI-powered development across its engineering projects.

At NVIDIA GTC 2025, General Motors presented an AI co-pilot built on the Neural Concept platform and trained on crash simulation data from 11 vehicle programs. Validated by GM’s engineers, it assesses a key pedestrian safety metric for new designs, turning what once took weeks of simulation into real-time feedback.
Pedestrian safety rarely sells a car. But it protects the people most exposed on the road.

For pedestrians and cyclists, the vehicle’s front end is their protection. In the US alone, a pedestrian was killed every 72 minutes in traffic crashes in 2023, according to NHTSA. Global standards such as GTR and NCAP make vulnerable road user protection a requirement for every new vehicle, for adults and children alike.

A single design iteration can take weeks, and safety competes with other attributes. A bumpier hood might better protect pedestrians, yet degrade aerodynamics, reduce range and clash with styling. When every extra iteration puts the program timeline at risk, designers may settle on a compromise where a better one could have been found.

Its engineers had a bold idea, drawn from the drag-reducing shape of a penguin’s fin. But turning biological inspiration into a high-performance industrial design takes a leap of faith and heavy engineering work. That’s where Neural Concept came in.
Aerospace is one of the hardest places to bring AI into engineering.

Aerospace also asks more of AI than most industries do. Aircraft noise is regulated, certification is demanding, and European aviation authorities are still working out how AI itself will be certified.

GTM Talent Acquisition Specialist

In the traditional process, that insight arrives in steps: engineers modify the geometry, launch simulations and assess results once the data becomes available. For JLR, the question was no longer model performance, but how to embed AI across real engineering systems with the robustness and traceability that production engineering demands.

Presented on stage at NVIDIA GTC, the results show AI working as part of JLR’s aerodynamic engineering, not beside it. Development is shifting from sequential execution toward continuous, data-driven decisions, with the repeatability and traceability needed to scale across vehicle programs.

In Leonardo’s helicopters and aircraft, a single design decision can carry years of consequence. On every programme, engineers would like to explore more alternatives than the time allows. Certification and design optimization require large numbers of simulations, while the industry faces growing pressure to shorten time-to-market as designs become more complex.
Every gram, every certification step and every test campaign carries a high cost. The programs that narrow the design space earliest let testing confirm rather than discover.
